name: Hydrolyzed silk protein

lead: Hydrolyzed silk protein is silk split into smaller peptides and amino acids, found in conditioners and cleansers. People use it for softer, smoother, shinier-looking hair.

Silk is mostly fibroin with a coating of sericin, and the small fragments are meant to coat the strands. It appears in patents for washing gels and permanent-wave compositions; no human study of hair appearance was found.

paras: It is used as an ingredient in conditioners, masks and cleansers, with the effect noticeable after each wash.
No hair-specific safety data were found in the sources reviewed.

studies.title: Feeding silk protein hydrolysates to C57BL/KsJ-db/db mice improves blood glucose and lipid profiles.

angle.text: Hydrolyzed silk protein is added to conditioners so small silk peptides coat the strands, leaving hair softer, smoother and glossier after use. Hair trials of the ingredient were not found.

lead: Hydrolyzed silk protein is silk protein broken into smaller peptides and amino acids, used in cosmetic products including hair conditioners and washes to leave hair and skin feeling smoother and softer. Silk is mainly fibroin with a coating of sericin.[1]
Cosmetic formulations containing it appear in patents for washing gels and permanent-wave compositions.[2][3] No clinical trial found tests it for hair appearance.

paras: Silk is about 75-80 percent fibroin with a glue-like sericin coating, though proportions vary by source.[1] Hydrolysis yields shorter protein fragments.

Patent documents list hydrolyzed silk protein as an ingredient in a bath foam-cream and a washing gel.[2][3] A 1989 permanent-waving patent combined hydrogen-bonding amino acids with a silicone compound to claim improved curl retention and hair feel.[4]
A 2010 study in diabetic mice examined silk protein hydrolysates for blood glucose and lipids.[5] It does not concern hair.

Wikipedia's article on sericin gives silk as about 70 to 80 percent fibroin, which forms the structural core of the fibre, and 20 to 30 percent sericin, the gum coating that holds fibres together. Sericin is roughly 32 percent serine, whose hydrogen bonds give it a glue-like quality [6]. The article reports that sericin can improve skin elasticity and have anti-wrinkle properties partly by reducing water loss from skin, and that it is used in wound closure for its biocompatibility. It does not discuss hair-care uses or hydrolyzed silk [6].

Hair conditioners do not biologically repair hair but deposit material that coats the fibre and fills damaged areas of the cuticle, reducing friction so hair combs more smoothly; cationic surfactants, fatty alcohols and silicones are the main agents described [7]. Hydrolyzed proteins are used in products on a similar premise, as small, water-soluble fragments that can sit on or in the hair surface, but the Wikipedia conditioner article does not single out silk protein [7].

In the patent record, hydrolyzed silk protein appears as one ingredient among surfactants and moisturisers: a 2005 Russian patent for a bath foam-cream lists it with sodium laureth sulfate and cocamidopropyl betaine, and a washing-gel patent lists it with panthenol and plankton extract as active additives [2][3].
No studies found for hair use.
